html:
The Dakota War of 1862 was a short war in southern Minnesota between the United States and the eastern bands of Dakota, the Santee: the Mdewakanton, Wahpekute, Sisseton and Wahpeton. It ended with the largest mass execution in American history.

In treaties of 1851 the Dakota had sold most of their land for payments and goods, keeping only a strip along the Minnesota River. By the summer of 1862 the payments were late, the Civil War had drawn off the government's attention, crops had failed and traders refused credit. Families were starving.

In August young Dakota men killed five settlers at Acton. Chief Little Crow, against his own judgment, agreed to lead a war. Dakota fighters attacked the agency, farms and towns, and killed several hundred settlers in a few weeks. Many Dakota refused to join, and some protected settlers. The army under Henry Sibley defeated the fighters at Wood Lake in late September, and most of the Dakota surrendered.

A military court sentenced 303 men to death after trials lasting minutes. President Lincoln cut the list, and 38 men were hanged together at Mankato on 26 December 1862. About 1,600 Dakota, mostly women and children, were held in a camp at Fort Snelling through the winter, where many died of disease. In 1863 Congress expelled the Dakota from Minnesota, and the army pursued those who fled onto the plains, beginning decades of war with the Sioux.
